Neonatal Moustached guenons (Cercopithecus cephus) emerge weighing approximately 340 grams [Wwb = approximately 340 grams], a modest birth mass that is typical for cercopithecine primates of this body plan. This initial size is markedly smaller than the ultimate adult dimensions attained later in life, reflecting the substantial growth trajectory required to reach mature body mass. Under captive conditions, adult females of this species achieve a maximum body weight of around 3400 grams [Wwi = around 3400 grams], whereas adult males are substantially larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 4100 grams [Wwi = 4100 grams]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males exceeding females by over 700 grams, is consistent with the polygynous mating system observed in many forest guenons, where larger body size confers advantages in male-male competitive interactions. The initial disparity between neonatal and adult mass underscores the extent of postnatal development that occurs as juveniles progress through the early life stages, from the neonatal period through the suckling phase and into full independence.

Gestation in the Moustached guenon has been documented at 172 days [tg = 172 days] under the standard thermoregulatory conditions characteristic of active, normothermic adult females, typically 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This duration is comparable to that reported for other medium-sized guenon species, reflecting the phylogenetic constraints on placental development and foetal growth within the genus Cercopithecus. After this five-and-a-half-month period of intrauterine development, parturition yields a single offspring, occasionally twins, that is entirely dependent on maternal care during the early neonatal stage. The internal fertilization event that initiates this process is followed by a sustained period of organogenesis and foetal growth within the uterine environment. Following birth, the neonate enters a prolonged suckling phase during which it relies entirely on the mother's milk for its nutritional needs, gradually developing the physiological capacity to process solid foods as it approaches weaning.

For juvenile Moustached guenons, weaning represents a pivotal nutritional transition that occurs at 365 days after birth [tx = 365 days after birth] under captive conditions maintained at 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This one-year period of lactation-dependent growth allows the newborn to acquire substantial mass and develop critical motor and social skills before achieving nutritional independence. After weaning, the juvenile enters a sub-adult phase characterized by continued somatic growth and increasing social integration within the troop. The transition to independent feeding involves a gradual shift from a milk-based diet to the adult omnivorous regimen of fruits, leaves, and small invertebrates. During this extended juvenile stage, individuals refine their foraging techniques through observational learning from older troop members. The steady accumulation of body mass and the development of adult dentition proceed in tandem, preparing the young primate for the eventual onset of reproductive maturity that will occur several years later, following a lengthy period of social and physical development.

Sexual maturation in the Moustached guenon is a gradual process, with puberty typically attained at 1460 days after birth [tp = 1460 days after birth] when animals are maintained at 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This corresponds to approximately four years of age, a timing that aligns well with the life-history schedules of other forest guenons and reflects the extended developmental period required for brain growth and social learning in this highly social primate. Upon reaching this developmental milestone, both males and females undergo significant endocrinological changes, including the onset of gametogenesis and the emergence of adult secondary sexual characteristics. For females, the first ovulation marks the initiation of cyclical ovarian activity and the potential for conception. Males, meanwhile, experience testicular enlargement and the commencement of spermatogenesis, though social maturity and successful breeding often occur somewhat later due to the complex dominance hierarchies that structure guenon societies. The interval between weaning and puberty thus represents a critical period of investment in both physical and social development.

Under optimal captive conditions with a stable core body temperature maintained at 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for Cercopithecus cephus extends to 36 years [am = 36 years]. This substantial longevity is characteristic of many Old World monkeys and reflects their relatively slow life-history pace, low extrinsic mortality rates in protected environments, and the complex neurobiological investment that accompanies their advanced cognitive abilities. Within this extended lifespan, the maximum reproductive rate for a breeding female is approximately one infant per birth [N_R_i = approximately one infant per birth], with births occurring roughly once every 2.5 years [F_R_i = births occurring roughly once every 2.5 years] under the described thermoregulatory regime. This low annual fecundity is typical of a K-selected life-history strategy, where each offspring receives intensive maternal investment over a prolonged period. The combination of late sexual maturation, extended interbirth intervals, and long lifespan positions the Moustached guenon firmly within the slow end of the primate life-history continuum.
